messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Memory → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Margarita was seventy years old, a fashion designer who still worked from the sunlit studio behind her Brooklyn brownstone, sketching collections that had once been shown on runways from Milan to São Paulo. The event that had shattered her life happened three years ago, on a February evening so cold the radiators in her building had groaned and clanked. She had been walking home from the subway when a man, wild-eyed and shouting in a language she did not understand, forced open the door of a bodega she was passing. She heard the gunshot. Through the glass, she saw the owner—a young man named Carlos who always remembered her order of café con leche—fall backward against the cooler. She had run inside, tried to press a towel to his chest, but his eyes had already gone still. The police came, then the news vans. The shooter was never caught. Carlos had no family in the country, and within a week the bodega was shuttered, the whole thing erased as if it had never happened.

In the months that followed, Margarita found that the memory of that night had a life of its own. It would rise without warning—the smell of spilled coffee and copper, the weight of Carlos’s body against her hands, the fluorescent light flickering above him. When it came, it was not a recollection but a full sensory reliving: she would feel the cold February air on her skin even if she was standing in her warm kitchen, and for a terrible moment she was there again, helpless, watching. The first time it happened at her sewing machine, she had stabbed her finger with a needle and not felt the pain until the blood spotted the silk.

She began to avoid things. The news was the worst—any report about an unsolved shooting, any mention of a bodega or a February night, and her heart would seize. She stopped watching television altogether, canceled her newspaper subscription, asked her husband to screen her phone calls. She also found herself pushing away any moment of warmth or joy—a compliment from a client, the smell of her granddaughter’s hair—because positive feelings felt dangerous, as if happiness made her vulnerable to the next sudden intrusion. The people responsible had faced no consequences, and this injustice gnawed at her. She had come to believe that she should have done more, that she should have pulled Carlos out of the store instead of running in, that the event had happened because of the way she had acted—too slow, too scared, too old. She had failed to protect him. Every time the memory surfaced, these appraisals grew sharper, and every time she blamed herself, the memory returned more vividly, as if her guilt were a summons.

The avoidance, she believed, kept her safe. But it also made the world smaller. Her husband began to find her standing in the middle of rooms, staring at nothing, her hands trembling. She stopped going to the neighborhood where the bodega had been, then stopped taking the subway altogether, then stopped leaving the studio except for necessities. One afternoon, a delivery man knocked too hard on her door, and she felt the cold February air on her skin again, the full memory crashing through her—the bodega, the gunshot, Carlos’s eyes. She had locked herself in the bathroom and wept. The lack of control over her own mind terrified her more than anything else. That evening, she told her husband she needed to see someone. What frightened her most was the thought that she would carry that February night inside her forever, that it would keep pulling her back until there was nothing left of the woman who had once designed dresses for women who danced.
